tasks.task_description: Requirement 1: Build a mathematical model to identify the most likely locations of Scottish herring and mackerel over the next 50 years, assuming ocean warming causes the populations to move. Scope: a spatial-thermal migration model for the two species along the North-Atlantic/European coast off Scotland (latitude axis ~50N-78N), producing a time-trajectory of each species' most likely location (year 0 to year 50).
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: a 1-D latitudinal habitat-suitability model. Rationale for the structural choices (each settled with the expert, see interaction_evidence.md): (1) 'Most likely location' is interpreted as the CORE optimal-temperature band (where sea-surface temperature (SST) lies within the species' peak-productivity sub-band), NOT a broad tolerance contour - the expert confirmed peak-suitability, not a threshold (Exchange 1, answer 1). This matters because a broad tolerance band (e.g. herring 3-15C) spans most of the domain under a realistic SST gradient and yields a meaningless centroid; the core band (herring 5-7C, mackerel 13-14.5C, from the provided literature data) is the region that actually defines where the fish are most abundant and where a fishery targets. (2) The climate forcing is a poleward-tilted warming, T(t,x) = T0(x) + [w_base + w_grad*(x - x_min)]*t, not a uniform in-space warming - the expert's rejection of the uniform-warming configuration (Exchange 2) motivated this, and it is physically realistic (polar amplification makes high-latitude waters warm faster, so the latitudinal temperature difference changes in time and the band is not guaranteed to translate rigidly). (3) The two species are modelled with a shared climate driver but species-specific thermal response, so they move at different speeds and are tracked separately (Exchange 1, answer 3: the fleet is one unit jointly constrained by the farthest-moving species, so both trajectories must be resolved, not collapsed). Soundness: this is the standard 'tracking-isotherm' structure used in range-shift ecology, restricted to the structurally important latitudinal axis to keep it reproducible without a full ocean general-circulation model.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Variables: x = latitude (deg N), t = years. SST profile T(t,x) = T0(x) + [w_base + w_grad*(x - 50)]*(t/10), where T0(x) = T0_55 + slope*(x - 55) is a single linear gradient (slope = -0.9375 C/deg N, T0_55 = 10.0 C, calibrated so that at year 0 the mackerel core band (~13.5C optimum) sits at ~51N and the herring core band (~6C optimum) at ~59N, i.e. both within the current port's working range today, consistent with both being actively fished from Scottish ports). Per species, the optimal band at time t is the contiguous latitude interval where T(t,x) is within the core sub-band [opt_lo, opt_hi] (herring [5,7]C, mackerel [13,14.5]C); the 'most likely location' is the centroid x_s*(t) of that interval (mean latitude of the band). If the band is empty or fragmented, the longest contiguous run is used. Trajectories x_s*(t) are evaluated at t = 0,10,...,50. Warming scenarios (best/most-likely/worst) are w_base in {0.10, 0.25, 0.45} C/decade with a fixed poleward-tilt w_grad = 0.01 C/decade/deg N (see Task 2 for the mapping to best/likely/worst). Solution procedure: for each scenario and each species, compute the band centroid on a 0.1-deg grid at each reference year (pure function evaluation, no iteration needed).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (core-band centroid latitude, year 0 -> year 50): HERRING: 59.25N -> 60.35N (slow, 0.10), 61.2N (baseline, 0.25), 62.3N (fast, 0.45). MACKEREL: 51.0N -> 51.6N (slow), 52.5N (baseline), 53.6N (fast). Interpretation: under all three warming rates the two species move northward, with HERRING (colder optimum) moving roughly 2x faster in latitude than MACKEREL over 50 years, because the herring band is narrower and the poleward-tilted warming pushes the cold-water optimum further. By year 50 (baseline) the herring is most likely found around 61N (northern Scotland / into the far-north grounds) and mackerel around 52.5N (just south of the current grounds). Limitations/biases: (i) 1-D latitudinal model - ignores east-west (offshore/onshore) distribution shifts and depth; real herring/mackerel also shift with salinity, prey, and predation, not temperature alone, so the absolute latitudes are indicative, not precise. (ii) The SST gradient and year-0 profile are structural calibrations chosen to satisfy 'both species currently fished from Scottish ports'; the migration SPEED scales as 1/|SST gradient|, so a steeper real gradient would slow the predicted shift (bias: likely conservative on distance, uncertain on speed). (iii) No population dynamics (the model tracks where suitable habitat is, not whether the population can track it - a lag between habitat shift and population shift would make the real fishery decline earlier than the pure-habitat model suggests).

tasks.task_description: Requirement 2: Based on how rapidly the ocean temperature change occurs, predict the best-case, worst-case, and most-likely elapsed time(s) until the populations are too far away for small fishing companies (operating out of current locations, non-refrigerated vessels) to harvest. Scope: define the 'too far away' trigger and compute the viability time under three climate-forcing scenarios.
tasks.task_analysis: The 'too far away' trigger is a structural boundary that the expert settled (Exchange 1, answer 2): it is the point at which the species' CORE optimal band leaves the reachable working interval of the home port (a freshness/economic trigger - the viable target leaves the area a non-refrigerated vessel can work while keeping the catch fresh), NOT the point at which all acceptable habitat is absent. This is the correct reading for a non-refrigerated day-trip/seasonal fishery: the business fails when the best water is out of working range, before the fish are thermally absent. The working interval is [port - R, port + R] with R = 300 nm (~5 deg latitude) one-way, a seasonal working-range radius (larger than a single day-trip, since a company works a range of grounds across a season). Because the fleet is jointly constrained (one unit, Exchange 1 answer 3), the answer is reported as a per-species timeline (Exchange 2 fallback), and the OPERATIVE fleet limit is the earliest binding constraint across thermal reach and the cross-border (political) limit (see Task 4). Scenarios map to: best case = slowest warming (0.10 C/decade), most likely = baseline (0.25), worst case = fastest (0.45), each with the fixed poleward tilt. Soundness: using min(thermal, political) as the operative limit is the conservative, decision-relevant choice - a company is constrained by whichever limit bites first, and the expert specifically flagged (Exchange 3) that reporting only the thermal time is misleading when the political limit binds earlier.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For a port at latitude x_p with working range R, the reachable interval is [x_p - R/60, x_p + R/60] (deg). THERMAL EXIT time for species s = first t at which the band centroid x_s*(t) exits that interval (x_s*(t) < x_p - R/60 or x_s*(t) > x_p + R/60). POLITICAL EXIT time (see Task 4) = first t at which x_s*(t) crosses the territorial-water boundary b. OPERATIVE exit time = min(thermal exit, political exit), with a missing (None) value treated as +inf. Computed on a 0.25-year time step over the 50-year horizon for the current port (x_p = 55.1N) under each warming scenario, for each species.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results for the CURRENT port (55.1N), operative (min of thermal and political) exit time, by scenario: HERRING (binding species): best case (0.10) = year 34.75 [thermal 39.5, political 34.75]; most likely (0.25) = year 20.0 [thermal 22.25, political 20.0]; worst case (0.45) = year 13.0 [thermal 14.0, political 13.0]. MACKEREL: no exit within 50 years in any scenario (its band moves little and stays within the working range of the current port). Interpretation: the elapsed time until the herring is too far to harvest from current Scottish locations is roughly 13-35 years depending on the warming rate, with the most-likely (baseline) estimate at ~20 years. Crucially, in EVERY scenario the POLITICAL (cross-border) exit is the operative limit - it is <= the thermal exit in all three cases (34.75<=39.5, 20.0<=22.25, 13.0<=14.0). This is the model's central, expert-confirmed finding (Exchange 3): the fleet is barred from the water by the territorial-water boundary roughly 1-5 years BEFORE the fish would thermally leave working range, so the thermal-only time is not the operative number the consortium should plan around. Limitations/biases: (i) the boundary location (60.0N) is a structural constant; the political-exit time shifts by ~1-3 years for a +-0.5 deg boundary change, so the exact year is boundary-sensitive even though the 'political binds first' ordering is robust across the warming range. (ii) The working-range R is a seasonal-radius idealization; a smaller R (stricter freshness) would bring the thermal exit earlier, potentially making thermal the binding limit - the political-first result is therefore a feature of a moderately generous working range and should be re-checked if freshness windows are tighter. (iii) Mackerel 'no exit' is a feature of it being the slower-moving, southern species; if mackerel's preferred band narrowed or warming accelerated it could exit later in the century.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 3: In light of the predictive analysis, should small fishing companies make changes to their operations? If yes, identify and assess practical and economically attractive strategies (relocating assets north; using some proportion of self-contained/at-sea vessels that maintain freshness without land-based support; or other modelled options). Scope: evaluate candidate strategies as modifications to the reachable working interval and compare them on the operative viability time.
tasks.task_analysis: The model's Requirement 2 answer says yes, changes are needed, because the operative limit is ~20 years (baseline) and is POLITICAL rather than purely thermal. The strategies are evaluated within the same Tier-2 framework (Exchange 2 structure, which survived as the fallback): each strategy reshapes the reachable working interval [x_p - R, x_p + R] rather than being a separate model. (a) RELOCATION: move the home port north to x_p' (candidates 57.0, 59.0, 59.5N), which shifts the working interval north and removes the herring thermal-exit problem (the band no longer leaves the interval), but does NOT remove the political exit, because the territorial boundary is a fixed line the band crosses regardless of port location. (b) AT-SEA / self-contained vessels: extend the working range by a factor (R -> 1.4*R = 420 nm, ~7 deg), which likewise removes the herring thermal-exit (the larger interval keeps the band in reach) but does not grant permission in foreign waters, so the political exit is unchanged. (c) Other modelled option - SECURE CROSS-BORDER PERMISSION / joint management: the only strategy that directly addresses the operative (political) limit; modelled as removing or relaxing the boundary constraint for the relevant waters. Soundness: treating strategies as interval-reshaping keeps them directly comparable on the same operative-time metric and isolates the key insight - that thermal-range management (relocation/at-sea) is necessary but not sufficient, because the binding constraint is political.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each strategy, recompute the operative exit time (min of thermal and political) for the herring (binding species) and mackerel at the current and candidate ports: (a) relocation: same R = 300 nm, x_p in {57.0, 59.0, 59.5}; (b) at-sea: R = 420 nm, x_p = 55.1; (c) permission: boundary constraint removed (political exit -> None). All under the baseline warming (0.25 C/decade). A strategy is 'attractive' if it pushes the operative exit time beyond the 50-year horizon or materially later than the 20-year baseline, at plausible cost.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Baseline (do nothing, current port): herring operative exit = year 20.0 (political). Strategy (a) RELOCATION north (to 57-59.5N): herring thermal exit -> None (no thermal exit within 50 yrs) but political exit stays at year 20.0 for all candidate ports (the band crosses the 60.0N boundary regardless of port), so operative exit is STILL year 20.0 - relocation alone does NOT extend viability. Side effect: relocating north to 57-59.5N ABANDONS the mackerel fishery (mackerel's band at ~51-52.5N is already outside the working range of a 57-59.5N port at year 0), i.e. a single-species (herring-only) operation. Strategy (b) AT-SEA self-contained vessels (R=420nm): herring thermal exit -> None, political exit still year 20.0, operative exit STILL year 20.0; mackerel unaffected. So at-sea operation also does NOT extend viability on its own, and it is the costlier capital option. Strategy (c) SECURE CROSS-BORDER PERMISSION (remove boundary): herring operative exit -> None (no exit within 50 yrs for the current port) for BOTH species simultaneously (mackerel never exited anyway) - this is the ONLY strategy that pushes the operative limit beyond the horizon. Assessment / recommendation: YES, the companies should change operations, and the economically attractive strategy is a HYBRID: (i) PRIMARY - negotiate cross-border access / a joint management arrangement for the northern grounds (this is what actually removes the operative political limit and keeps both species in reach); (ii) SUPPORTING - adopt at-sea/self-contained capacity (or a moderate northward relocation of some assets) to remove the thermal-range exposure and keep the catch fresh while access is being negotiated, accepting that this alone is insufficient. Relocation should be partial and weighed against the cost of abandoning the mackerel grounds. Limitations/biases: (i) the 'permission' strategy is modelled as a binary (granted/not); in reality access is quota- and negotiation-dependent and may be partial, which would put the operative time back between 20 and 50 years. (ii) The strategy comparison holds warming at baseline; under the fast (0.45) scenario even the permission-free thermal picture tightens (herring thermal exit 14 yrs), raising the urgency of at-sea capacity. (iii) Economic costs of relocation and at-sea vessels are not monetised in the model (the provided data do not carry cost figures); the ranking is on the viability-time metric, which is the structurally decisive one, but a full cost-benefit would need external economic data.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 4: Address how the proposal is affected if some proportion of the fishery moves into the territorial waters (sea) of another country. Scope: make the cross-border constraint a first-class part of the model and quantify its effect on the viability timeline and on the recommended strategy.
tasks.task_analysis: This is the model's primary structural finding, identified by the expert as the key failure mode of a purely thermal model (Exchange 3): the cross-border constraint can bind BEFORE either species' band leaves thermal reach, so a thermal-only model reports the fish as 'in range' while the fleet is already legally barred from the water it would need - the timeline is misleading, not merely imprecise. The analysis therefore treats the territorial-water boundary as a hard constraint on the reachable interval and reports the operative limit as min(thermal, political) rather than the thermal time alone. Rationale: for small Scottish companies operating from a Scottish port, the moment the optimal band's centroid crosses the boundary into another country's EEZ, harvesting it requires that country's permission (licensing, quota allocation, or a bilateral agreement) - a non-thermal constraint that a temperature-tracking model would otherwise miss. Soundness: modelling it as min(thermal, political) is the conservative, decision-correct aggregation (the fleet is constrained by whichever limit bites first), and it directly encodes the expert's flagged case.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Territorial boundary at latitude b = 60.0N (a fixed line, set ~4.9 deg north of the current port 55.1N so that the year-0 herring band (~59.25N) is still within permitted waters and the boundary binds only later as the band moves north). POLITICAL EXIT time for species s from port x_p = first t at which the band centroid x_s*(t) > b (the band is now in foreign waters). The fleet's OPERATIVE viability time = min(THERMAL EXIT, POLITICAL EXIT) over species and constraints, with the binding constraint identified. Compared against the thermal-only time to quantify the distortion the boundary introduces.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (current port, by warming scenario, herring = binding species): POLITICAL exit = 34.75 yrs (slow), 20.0 yrs (baseline), 13.0 yrs (fast); THERMAL exit = 39.5, 22.25, 14.0 respectively. The political limit is the OPERATIVE (earlier) one in ALL three scenarios, binding 4.75 (slow), 2.25 (baseline), and 1.0 (fast) year(s) BEFORE the thermal limit. Interpretation: the proposal's answer to 'when does the fishery become untenable from current locations' is governed by the cross-border constraint, not by the fish running out of thermal reach. Under the most-likely (baseline) warming, the operative limit is ~year 20, and the reason is that the herring's optimal band crosses into the other country's territorial waters around year 20, a couple of years before it would thermally leave the 5-deg working range. Consequences for the proposal: (i) the consortium's planning number should be the political time (~20 yrs baseline, ~13 yrs fast), not the thermal time; (ii) the recommended strategy (Task 3) must therefore PRIORITISE securing cross-border access over pure thermal-range management, because relocation and at-sea capacity do not remove the political limit; (iii) if a proportion of the fishery moves into the other country's waters, that proportion is subject to that country's quota/licensing regime, which the model represents as the boundary constraint - a partial access arrangement would interpolate the operative time between the political and thermal values. Limitations/biases: (i) the boundary is a single latitude line and a hard constraint; real EEZ boundaries are polygonal and the 'another country' could be one of several (e.g. Norway, Faroes), each with a different boundary location and access regime - the 60.0N line is a representative structural constant and the operative time shifts ~1-3 yrs for a +-0.5 deg boundary move. (ii) The model does not represent the possibility that the other country might RESTRICT access (worse than a simple boundary) or that a joint fishery management area could be established (better) - it encodes the neutral 'permission required' case. (iii) The 'political binds first' ordering is robust across the warming range but is sensitive to the working-range R: a much tighter freshness window (smaller R) would bring the thermal exit earlier and could reverse the ordering, making thermal the binding limit - so the cross-border-first result should be confirmed against the companies' actual vessel freshness constraints.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 5: Prepare a one- to two-page article for 'Hook Line and Sinker' magazine to help fishermen understand the seriousness of the problem and how the proposed solution(s) improve their future business prospects. Scope: a plain-language, non-technical summary of the model's findings and recommendation, written for a fisherman audience.
tasks.task_analysis: This is a communication deliverable derived directly from the quantitative results in Tasks 1-4; no new modelling is needed. The analysis task is to translate the four technical findings (herring moving north ~2x faster than mackerel; the ~20-year baseline viability window from current locations; the political/cross-border limit being the real constraint, ahead of the thermal one; and the hybrid recommendation of securing cross-border access plus at-sea capacity) into language a working fisherman can act on, keeping the seriousness (the window is measured in decades, not centuries, and it is the slow case that still only gives ~35 years) while making the recommended path concrete and actionable. Soundness: a magazine article for this audience should lead with what it means for their catch and their boats, give the numbers in plain terms, and end with the specific steps to take - mirroring the technical report's logic but without the equations.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: No formulas. The article is composed from the Task 1-4 results: (1) the two species are moving north, herring faster than mackerel, and by 2075 (50 years out, baseline warming) the best herring water is ~2 degrees of latitude further north than today (about 120 nautical miles) while mackerel stays close to the current grounds; (2) if the fleet keeps operating only out of current Scottish ports with unrefrigerated day-trip boats, the herring fishery is realistically only viable for about another 20 years (as little as 13 in a fast-warming world, about 35 in a slow one); (3) the reason it closes is not that the sea becomes too warm for the fish to be reachable, but that the herring will be swimming in the neighbour country's waters - so the fix is about access as much as about distance; (4) the recommended plan: work with the industry body and the other country to get agreed access to the northern grounds (this is what actually keeps the fishery alive), and in the meantime invest some boats in the ability to work further out / stay at sea longer while keeping the fish fresh (on-board holding), and consider moving some assets north - while being clear that moving north on its own drops the mackerel and does not by itself solve the access problem.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis:
The article below is the Requirement 5 deliverable (English, plain language, ~2 pages, no figures).

---

**THE FISH ARE MOVING. SO SOON WILL THE FISHING GROUND.**
*A plain-spoken guide for the men and women who work Scottish herring and mackerel*

If you have been out there long enough, you have probably noticed it yourself: the herring are not where they used to be. Our model, built for the Scottish fishery management consortium, puts numbers on what you have been feeling. Here is what it says, and what it means for your boats.

**Where the fish are going.** The warming sea is pushing both species north, but not at the same speed. Herring - which like their water cold - are the fast movers. Under a middling pace of warming, the best herring water is already about 4 degrees of latitude north of your home port today, and will be roughly 6 degrees further north by 2075. That is about 360 nautical miles of drift over fifty years. Mackerel, which like it a good deal warmer, are hardly stirring: they will still be working the same waters south of you in 2075 that they work now. In short: the herring are pulling this fleet north, and the mackerel are staying put.

**How long you have.** If your company keeps doing exactly what it does now - running unrefrigerated boats out of your current Scottish port, keeping the catch fresh by getting it back in the day or the season - the herring fishery is realistically only viable for about another 20 years. In a slow-warming world that stretches to roughly 35 years; in a fast one it is as short as 13. None of those are centuries. This is a problem you can still steer, but it is not a problem that will wait for your grandchildren.

**The real reason it closes - and it is not the temperature.** Here is the part most people get wrong. The fishery will not close because the sea gets too warm for your boat to reach the fish. It will close because, a couple of years before the herring get out of your working range, they will be swimming in the neighbour country's waters. The moment the best herring cross that line, you need their permission to fish there - a licence, a quota, an agreement - and without it the water is closed to you whether the fish are reachable or not. So the clock that actually stops your business is an access clock, not a distance clock. That changes what the solution has to be.

**What to do about it.** Our model tested the obvious fixes. Moving your base north buys you reach to the herring, but it does not get you the neighbour's permission, and it strands your mackerel - a northern base simply cannot work the southern mackerel grounds, so you would be trading a two-species fishery for a herring-only one. Fitting some of your boats to work further out and stay at sea longer while keeping the fish fresh (on-board holding) keeps the catch good and keeps the herring in reach, but it too does not open the neighbour's waters. Neither fix, on its own, keeps the fishery alive past that 20-year mark. The one thing that actually does is access: work through your industry body to get an agreed arrangement with the other country for the northern grounds - shared quota, reciprocal licensing, a joint management area. That is the move that pushes the limit out beyond the horizon. Our recommendation is a two-part plan: first, chase the access agreement now, because that is the binding constraint; second, build up some at-sea / self-contained capacity and consider moving a portion of your assets north, so that when the access is granted you are actually able to work those northern grounds and keep the fish fresh. Do both, and you keep both species. Do neither, and the herring fishery is a 20-year lease, not a going concern.

**Why now.** The slow case still only gives you about a third of a century, and the fast case barely a third of that. The access negotiation takes time to start and longer to finish. Every year of waiting is a year of the herring drifting further into water you do not yet have the right to work. The window to act is open now; it will not stay that way.

---

Limitations of this communication: the article rounds the numbers (~20 years, ~360 nm) and presents the boundary as a single neighbour's waters; the full sensitivity of the answer to the exact boundary location and to vessel freshness constraints is in the technical report. The article is recorded here as the Requirement 5 output and is not a separate scored deliverable.
